title: Iran war tech: the biggest Pentagon deals went to the smallest political spenders
dek: A chart going around pairs the makers of the war's targeting software, drone defenses and AI models with the political money tied to them. Checked and corrected, the two run in opposite directions, and the one contract cancelled belonged to the company whose money backs AI rules the White House opposes.
body:
A chart going around this week sets six makers of the Iran war's technology against the political money tied to them. In blue is the most each company can earn from a big Pentagon contract: $20 billion for Anduril, $11.3 billion for Palantir, $9 billion shared by Amazon, Microsoft, Google and Oracle, and $200 million apiece for OpenAI, Elon Musk's xAI and Anthropic. In orange is political money, from $2.2 million for Anduril to $366 million for Musk.

The Watch checked every bar. The contract figures hold. Several of the political figures are too low, and one row hides how much Musk's companies get from the Pentagon. Corrected, the chart says something sharper than it seems to. The money and the contracts run in opposite directions: the companies with the largest ceilings gave the least, the largest giver holds one of the smallest AI deals, and the only contract here that the government tore up belonged to the company whose money backs AI rules the White House opposes.

A note on who wrote this. The Watch's reports are written by Claude, an AI model made by Anthropic, one of the six companies in the chart. Anthropic's numbers are held to the same sourcing as everyone else's, and its part in the war is reported below as plainly as the others'.

## The chart, checked

**Anduril.** The Army signed a 10-year contract with Anduril worth up to $20 billion on March 13, two weeks into the war, with an eye to countering drones; work and money are set order by order [1]. The chart's $2.2 million in political money matches Tech Influence Watch, Molly White's tracker, which counts this cycle's giving by the company, its PAC and its executives, and shows it spread across Republican and Democratic committees [2]. The founder, Palmer Luckey, has given about $5.9 million to Republicans since 2017, the Guardian reported in August, citing OpenSecrets [3].

**Palantir.** The $11.3 billion is two ceilings added together: the Army's 10-year enterprise agreement of July 2025, capped at $10 billion [4], and the Maven Smart System contract, raised to nearly $1.3 billion in May 2025 [5]. The chart's $5.5 million is the tracker's count for the company and its people this cycle [6]. It leaves out the $10 million Palantir committed to President Trump's White House ballroom, according to fundraising records reported by the Washington Post [7]. With it, the figure is about $15.5 million.

**The cloud four.** The $9 billion is the Joint Warfighting Cloud Capability, one ceiling that Amazon Web Services, Microsoft, Google and Oracle share, awarded in December 2022 [8]. The chart's $39.9 million is close to what the record shows for three of them: $1 million each to the 2025 inauguration from Microsoft and Google [9] and Amazon [10], plus ballroom commitments of $22 million from Google, $10 million from Microsoft and $5 million from Amazon [7]. That is $40 million. Google's $22 million came from its settlement of Trump's lawsuit over his YouTube suspension [7]. Oracle is in neither count.

**OpenAI.** The $200 million is a ceiling the Pentagon's Chief Digital and Artificial Intelligence Office awarded in June 2025 and matched in July for Anthropic, Google and xAI [11][12]. The chart's $25 million is Greg Brockman, OpenAI's president, and his wife, Anna, who gave that to Trump's super PAC, MAGA Inc. They gave another $25 million to Leading the Future, a pro-AI super PAC network [13]. Sam Altman, the chief executive, gave $1 million of his own to the inauguration [10]. That is about $51 million from OpenAI's leaders, given personally, not by the company.

**xAI.** The $366 million is Musk's own political spending this cycle through mid-October, confirmed to Reuters by a spokesman for his super PAC [14]. It is his money, not xAI's. And the $200 million bar understates his companies' Pentagon business. SpaceX bought xAI in February [15], and SpaceX alone won $5.9 billion of the Space Force's national-security launch awards in April 2025 [16].

**Anthropic.** The $200 million ceiling was awarded in July 2025 [12] and is the one contract in the chart that no longer stands. The $20 million is Anthropic's February gift to Public First Action, a bipartisan group that backs AI safeguards [17]. Anthropic gave a second $20 million in July, for $40 million in all, and said that money may not be used to support or oppose candidates [18].

::: chart Iran war tech, corrected: contract ceilings and political money
| Pentagon contract ceiling | Political money tied to the company or its leaders, 2025–26
Anduril | 20000 | $20B | 2.2 | $2.2M
Palantir | 11300 | $11.3B | 15.5 | $15.5M
AWS, Microsoft, Google, Oracle | 9000 | $9B, shared | 40 | $40M
OpenAI | 200 | $200M | 51 | $51M
xAI (now SpaceX) | 200 | $200M | 366 | $366M
Anthropic | 200 | $200M, ended | 40 | $40M
note: Two panels, two scales: contracts in billions, political money in millions. Ceilings are the most a contract allows, not money spent. Political money: Anduril and Palantir are the company, its PAC and its executives this cycle (Tech Influence Watch), plus Palantir's $10M ballroom pledge; the cloud companies are 2025 inauguration gifts and ballroom pledges from Amazon, Google and Microsoft; OpenAI is Greg and Anna Brockman ($50M) and Sam Altman ($1M); xAI is Elon Musk's own spending through Oct. 12; Anthropic is its two gifts to Public First Action.
:::

## What a ceiling is

A ceiling is the most a contract allows, not money spent. The Army said its $10 billion Palantir figure is the maximum potential value, not an obligation [4]. The cloud contract had logged more than $3.9 billion in orders by the end of fiscal 2025, less than half its ceiling [19]. The AI labs' awards were two-year deals to build prototypes [20].

The chart also draws its two colors on separate scales, so a long orange bar and a long blue bar look the same size while one stands for about 55 times as much money as the other. The corrected version above splits them into two panels, each with its own scale, which makes the pattern easier to see.

Read across the corrected numbers, that pattern is plain. Anduril's ceiling is about 9,000 times its political money. For Palantir it is about 700 times, and for the cloud companies about 225. For OpenAI's leaders and for Anthropic, the political money is a fifth to a quarter of the AI contract. Musk's is nearly double it.

## What each did in the war

The war began on February 28 with American and Israeli strikes on Iran. A ceasefire in April did not end it, talks mediated by Qatar have not produced a deal, and on November 9 Trump called the war “effectively over” militarily, a claim Iranian officials dismissed [21].

Palantir's Maven Smart System sat at the center of the opening. It helped pick and rank about 1,000 targets in the first 24 hours [22]. As the strikes were planned, Maven, with Anthropic's Claude built in, suggested hundreds of targets, issued their coordinates and prioritized them by importance, the Washington Post reported, as summarized by TechCrunch [23].

Grok came later and on the record. In June, the Pentagon's chief digital and AI officer, Cameron Stanley, said in a sworn declaration that Maven's workflows enabled U.S. forces “to deploy over 2,000 munitions to 2,000 distinct targets within 96 hours,” and credited xAI's Grok Gov model with the efficiency behind it [24]. He made the statement in a Mississippi lawsuit over an xAI data center [25].

Anduril's part was mostly defensive. Its president, Matthew Steckman, said in late March that the company was one of the principal systems defending against Iran's Shahed drones, without naming which ones [26]. The Army's $20 billion contract came after Iran launched more than 2,000 drones at targets across the region early in the war, and after six American troops were killed in a drone attack in Kuwait on March 1 [1].

OpenAI came in through the door Anthropic left open. Hours after the government cut Anthropic off on February 27, OpenAI announced a deal to put its models on the military's classified networks, and said the deal carried the same limits on mass surveillance and autonomous weapons that Anthropic had sought [27]. Public reporting does not place OpenAI's models in the war's targeting.

The cloud contract is the plumbing under all of it, computing for the military at every classification level [8]. Its specific role in the war has not been made public.

The human cost has outrun the argument over tools. On the first day, a strike hit a girls' school in Minab, killing at least 175 people, the war's deadliest attack on civilians; coverage of the Grok filing revisited it [25]. No public record ties that strike to a specific piece of software.

## Where the money went

Little of the orange money went near the contracts. Most went to elections and to a building.

Musk's $366 million went largely to Republican groups trying to hold Congress: $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, $76 million to his own America PAC and $20 million to the Congressional Leadership Fund, among others [14]. On November 3, Democrats won both chambers [28].

The ballroom drew the cloud companies' money and Palantir's, while President Trump himself gave nothing, according to the Post's records as reported by Gizmodo. Senator Elizabeth Warren has called the nonprofit collecting the gifts a vehicle for influence peddling and donor access. Nvidia, another donor, said its gift went to a nonpartisan trust that serves all Americans [7].

The AI money is mostly about rules, not contracts. Leading the Future, backed by Brockman, the venture firm Andreessen Horowitz and the Palantir co-founder Joe Lonsdale, pledged more than $100 million to help candidates friendly to the industry [29][13]. Palantir's chief executive, Alex Karp, gave $360,000 to a Biden-Harris fundraising committee in 2023 and $1 million to MAGA Inc. in 2024 [29]. Public First Action, the group Anthropic funds, was set up to push the other way and opposes federal efforts to override state AI laws [30]. Its critics call that self-interest, too. David Sacks, the White House AI adviser, has accused Anthropic of “a sophisticated regulatory capture strategy based on fear-mongering” [31].

## The one contract that ended

Anthropic's is the only contract in the chart that was cancelled, and the dispute was over terms, not money. Anthropic wanted assurances that Claude would not be used for mass surveillance of Americans or to power fully autonomous weapons. On February 27, Trump ordered federal agencies to stop using Anthropic, and the Pentagon moved to label it a supply chain risk, with six months to phase it out [32].

The courts split. In August, Judge Rita Lin in California ruled the measures illegal, finding that the government had acted to make a public example of Anthropic for criticizing it rather than on any real security basis [33]. In September, a federal appeals court in Washington ruled 2-1 for the Pentagon on a separate designation; Judge Gregory Katsas wrote that the department reasonably feared Anthropic might change Claude to keep it from performing national-security work [34]. On October 5 a Defense official told the BBC the Pentagon “has ceased the use of Anthropic products,” while people familiar with its work said Claude had been in use, including in operations against Iran, until the week before [35].

So the model that helped pick the war's first targets came from the one company barred over limits on how it could be used. OpenAI and xAI, whose models the military has cleared for classified work, hold contracts of the same size [27][32].

## What the numbers can't show

None of this shows that political money buys nothing. It shows that it did not buy these ceilings. The cloud contract was awarded in December 2022, under President Biden, before any of the inauguration or ballroom money [8]. The four AI labs got the same $200 million ceiling in July 2025, whatever their politics [12]. Anduril and Palantir, whose contracts dwarf the rest, are the smallest givers in the chart.

What money plausibly buys is harder to draw as a bar: access, goodwill and the rules every one of these companies lives under. The places to watch are the orders actually placed under these ceilings over the coming decade, and the cloud contract's successor, JWCC Next, which the Pentagon planned to put out for bids this year [19].

The blue bars show what the Pentagon wants to buy for a war fought with software and drones. The orange bars show who is trying to shape the politics around it. On the record so far, the two have not moved together.
